[h1][i]“I can’t help but feel I’ve been ripped off.”[/i]
~Guybrush Threepwood[/h1]

The story of [b]Bill Tiller[/b] is... Kinda sad when you think about it. Then again, many others ended up the same way. People we used to worship back in the days ended up losing all of our trust and all the cult status. [b]Peter Molyneux[/b], who gave us games like [b]Dungeon Keeper[/b], [b]Black & White[/b] and [b]Fable[/b], ended up being a fraud and a liar who scam people on [b]Kickstarter[/b] with his empty promises. [b]Brian Fargo[/b], a man behind [b]Wasteland[/b] and the original [b]Fallout[/b] came pretty close by accumulating millions on, you guessed it, [b]Kickstarter[/b], and then making cheap-ass games, while also starting a shady video game store that revolves around cryptocurrency. [b]Richard Garriott[/b], the legendary [b]Lord British[/b], creator of bloody [b]Ultima[/b] and, while we're at it, the whole RPG genre went to [b]Kickstarter[/b] too. They're still suing his space-traveling ass. The biggest fraud in gaming history, [b]Star Citizen[/b], is run by [b]Chris Roberts[/b], creator of [b]Wing Commander[/b] series. And yes, you guessed it, it all started with [b]Kickstarter[/b]. The list continues, but you've got the idea. Now, what about [b]Bill[/b]?

You know, [b]Bill[/b]. The lead artist of [b]LucasArts[/b]' [b]The Dig[/b], who also worked on games like [b]Full Throttle[/b], [b]Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine[/b] and, of course, [b]The Curse of Monkey Island[/b]. Unfortunately, when [b]LucasArts[/b] hired EA exec, he, according to himself, started to feel like the team started to lose its creative freedom. The team was great, but that new EA exec guy (again, according to [b]Bill[/b]) “just didn't get it”. [b]Bill[/b] left, leaving one of the most influential developers in a history of point-and-click adventures behind, and joined [b]ArenaNet[/b], who were working on their now famous MMORPG [b]Guild Wars[/b]. [b]Bill[/b] praised their skills in his interview, [i]but[/i] working on MMO proved to be heavily different from what he was used to ([b]Arena[/b] guys didn't have finished concept to make arts for) [i]and[/i]... You guessed it. [b]Bill[/b] didn't like taking orders from a “programmer who didn't know anything about art”. He left again. This time, though, he co-founded his own company called [b]Autumn Moon Entertainment[/b].

Their first game was [b]A Vampyre Story[/b]. And you know what? It wasn't bad. Visually it was totally fine and stylish, the characters were likable, there were tons of quality-of-life features like walk skipping, we were able to turn into a bat and like I said, it wasn't bad at all. Except it was poorly made. The game used a free engine called [b]Panda3D[/b], had quite a lot of bugs on launch, etc. Also, even with free engine behind it, [b]Bill[/b] and his new team didn't manage to achieve much – the game ended abruptly with no ending and no explanation why. In other words, the game was left unfinished. And instead of fixing things in a sequel, [b]Bill[/b] started to work on prequel. Moreover, [b]A Vampyre Story: Year One[/b] was supposed to be episodic game. Because obviously, such games are easier to produce and make more money. Talking about money. It was then when [b]Bill[/b] discovered that evil thingy I've mentioned above, the [b]Kickstarter[/b]. Nobody really wanted yet another generic point-and-click game, though, and [b]A Vampyre Story[/b] simply wasn't special enough to get the attention, so... Yeah. No money – no game. [b]A Vampyre Story: Year One[/b] didn't happen. A couple of years before that, though, [b]Bill[/b] made another game with the [b]Autumn Moon[/b]. That game was [b]Ghost Pirates of Vooju Island[/b].

What can I say? He desperately tried to milk the time he spent working on third [b]Monkey Island[/b] there. He never worked on the first two, which are considered to be “true” [b]Monkey Island[/b], but still, he got that certain reputation and, well, he tried to turn it into money. Didn't work out either. Despite using the same exact engine with [b]A Vampyre Story[/b], [b]Ghost Pirates[/b] had rather terrible puzzles (it was one of those games that forced us to use some random things on some other random things, just because logic wasn't involved most of the time), quite a lot of quality-of-life features disappeared (for example, there was no way to skip walks), while [b]Gobliiins[/b]-like multiple characters approach only made all the above worse. The worst of all, though, it was a terribly made game that crashed a lot and do some other nasty things. Which is very ironic when you think about it. Can't make a good game without learning how to work in a team, huh?

Unfortunately, [b]Kickstarter[/b] didn't go anywhere. Money were there, waiting to be taken. With [b]A Vampyre Story: Year One[/b] in mind, it was decided not to ask much this time. They only asked $40.000 and, well, they've got it. So, here we are. In a company of [b]Duke Grabowski, Mighty Swashbuckler[/b]. And you know what? It's not nearly as poorly made as the previous [b]Autumn Moon[/b] efforts. It looks like the team actually cared. Why? Because they had a share. See, this game was only technically made by [b]Autumn Moon[/b]. [b]AM[/b] owned [b]Ghost Pirates[/b], this here technically is a spin-off (no, you don't need to play [b]Ghost Pirates[/b] first), team wanted a share, hence the financial hocus pocus – the team registered their own name, [b]Venture Moon[/b], and [b]Bill[/b] licensed the IP to them, while still leading the project and doing things like writing and art directing.

That's the saddest thing here, though. The whole thing is about money. Nobody wanted to make statement. Nobody wanted to make art. It was just that – they've got 40K and they needed to deliver a product. You may say that you can't make anything solid with only 40K and you're right, you can't. [b]Attic Door Productions[/b] (the guys behind [b]The 13th Doll[/b]) barely managed with 60 and since they actually cared about their project, they ended up adding a lot from their own wallets. [b]Bill[/b] and his team did not. Thanks to which we've got... only eight screens. That's right, guys, the whole game is only eight screens. And it's not like there's a lot of things to do there. You just press [b]Tab[/b] to see what you can interact with and then do just that – click on things. No thinking involved. Don't get me wrong, I do appreciate logic (hello, [b]Ghost Pirates[/b]), but it is [i]not[/i] about logic here. It's about lack of content. At very best you'll have a couple of objects in your inventory at the same time (won't even be real items, since the game utilizes the same ol' ideas from previous games and lets you carry the “ideas” with you) and it'll be painfully obvious where to use 'em. It's one of those games that don't even need a guide. Just because of how obvious everything is. Thanks to which you can beat the whole thing in less than an hour if you won't listen to each and every line completely (like in [b]Ghost Pirates[/b], you can't skip walks, but at least dialogues are skippable). Maybe the story's good? Nope. Again, [b]Bill[/b] tried to pull his “I've worked on [b]Monkey Island[/b]!” thing. And again, he failed. [b]Duke Grabovsky[/b] feels like something from that “We've got X at home” meme. More sad than funny.

So... Ye-e-ah. Eight screens, about 30 minutes of pure gameplay (again, if you won't listen to dialogues) and lame attempts to imitate [b]Monkey Island[/b]. Music from [b]Ghost Pirates[/b] and free assets included. That would be $40.000. Like I said, though, [b]Duke Grabovsky[/b] is not a terribly made game. The guys switched to another free engine, [b]Unity[/b], with [b]Adventure Creator[/b] toolkit, which leads to the game being stable and running in modern resolutions, but still, what we have here is not really a game, but an excuse for [b]Kickstarter[/b] campaign. What can I say? At least it was $40.000, not $700.000.000.

[h1] Duke Grabowsky, Mighty Swashbuckler Review [/h1]

[h3] A short, cute and funny point and click adventure gem, reminiscence of old school [b]Monkey Island[/b] style games[/h3]

I bought this game cheap, can't even remember exactly when or whether it was directly from steam or a 3rd party store, doesn't really matter, I went in without too much expectations but a little bit of hope, and I wasn't disappointed.

[b]Duke Grabowsky, Mighty Swashbuckler[/b] is a fun, yet extremely short and not very difficult classic point & click adventure game, the controls are so simple it really reminds me of the original Monkey Island games or even Simon The Sorcerer, the game is fun to play, the voice acting is very well made and the game made me chuckle and even laught at a few occasions.

The graphic style is nothing special, it's modern enough to look good and toy-ish enough to fit the story, which is from the get-go not a very serious one, the game doesn't take itself too seriously and that's a good thing, it comes off as a lightheaded, comically fun pirate adventure.

I won't say too much about the story or the characters themself so not to give any spoilers, but I really enjoyed the game, even though I finished it in under 2 hours overall playtime, including all achievements.

Overall, I definitely recommend this game for those who loves the classic point & click adventure, and want a good chuckle while they play, [b]7/10[/b] from me.

were making and thanked all that contributed to production, including donors.

Cons:
- Short length. While it's understandable due to the premise
of the game, I wish there were more.
- There are times when characters are walking and it looks like
they're walking too slowly for their speed to suggest.
- This one is just a personal preference, but during the ending cutscene,
a few of the woman's breasts jiggle even when the movements didn't
seem to warrant such a reaction. I understand this game is about wooing
a few ladies. But it seemed a tad excessive.
- I never got to order a drink at the Ben Plunder Inn. I really wanted to
sample his libations and the game just won't let me. What gives?

Conclusion:
It's a good game if you want to pick up a quick point and click
game that's more mature than a Humungous Entertainment game
with all the humor and anachronistic charms of Monkey Island. Pirates
and point and click adventures just seem to go together like peanut butter
and jelly and Duke Grabowski, Mighty Swashbuckler is one such example.

Estamos ante un juego de point and clic, que recuerda mucho (por no decir roba) a Monkey Island, aunque es de una calidad bastante inferior tanto técnica como jugablemente, pero que con sus defectos y todo termina siendo disfrutable (y esta a un precio acorde a lo que propone). 
Nos toca encarnar a un pirata que quiere ser capitán de su barco y, para probarles al resto de la tripulación que podemos serlo, debemos "enamorar" a tres mujeres. Esa es toda la premisa, no tiene más, lo más importante es el apartado jugable.
Sobre este debemos comentar que se trata de un titulo sin tanta complejidad como los ya mencionados Monkey Island, cada objeto con el que podemos interaccionar solo nos da tres opciones (hablar, ver y tocar) y nunca vamos a tener muchas cosas en el inventario como para tenerlo cargado. Es por esa razón que es un juego más simple, con puzzles no muy complejos, pero sigue siendo una experiencia disfrutable, en la que no nos vamos a quedar atorados por horas (o hasta que nos rindamos y busquemos en internet que hacer).
Si nunca jugaste ningún juego del tipo, este es bueno para probar ya que no se vuelve frustrante en ningún momento ni te deja encerrado en ninguna parte (ademas, es un juego cortito, me lo terminé en menos de 3 horas, haciendo todo lo que el juego ofrece). 
El juego no esta en español, pero por internet se consigue una traducción.
Si todo lo que comente no es un impedimento para que lo pruebes y podes tolerar su apartado técnico (que se queda corto hasta para principios de los 2000), es una experiencia interesante que recomiendo. BottomLine at the Top:  This game is to Monkey Island what Orville is to Star Trek.  A fantastic P&C adventure whose only flaw is that it ends so, so quickly.


-------------------------------------
Pros
-------------------------------------
-Top level P&C production values.  Art, voice acting, music, and dialogue are all excellent.
-Runs well at high resolution on systems that are more moderately powered (i.e. mine.)
-Detailed environments with lots of stuff to click on and hear Duke's bizarre descriptions.
-Double click exit to next screen/room.
-Autosaves.
-The use of other characters skills as inventory "items" as well as leaving items in inventory as idea bubbles before you have an idea for what to do with them is a unique mechanic for a P&C game.  
-Large voice cast.
-Easy to get 100% completion.


-------------------------------------
Meh.
-------------------------------------
-Not a lot of inventory usage.  I chalk part of this up to the game obviously being cut short from its originally intended length.  Had the game been longer I expect this to have been less of an issue.


-------------------------------------
Cons
-------------------------------------
-Again, the biggest drawback to this game is its abrupt ending.  It ends just as the story feels like it’s starting to really pick up and it leaves the whole thing just feeling unfinished.
-Character animations do not lip sync well to voice recordings.  Also (as other reviewers have mentioned) the characters often stare out into the distance when talking to each other.  I am not sure if these things were a stylistic choice or a design compromise but either way it does take away from what would otherwise be one of the highest production quality P&C games that I have seen in a while.
 

I was not able to figure out the backstory as to why the development of this game was cut short.  My main theory is that they simply ran out of money.  Producing a P&C game of this quality with an original character for an independent game developer is extremely ambitious.  I think they should at the very least be commended for following through on the game play that they were able to create for their crowdfunders.  Many P&C's that start as crowdfunded projects ultimately just fall through the cracks with zero to show for their backers’ investments. 
$2 regular asking price for approximately 2 hours of game play is not a bad deal for a game whose only drawback is that there is not more of it to play. All in all, it has the feel of a great Monkey Island game, which should make it a must buy for any P&C adventure fan.  As long as you go into it knowing that it’s going to end sooner than you want it to, I'd say give it a try!

Cosa dire di questo gioco. Che non è una normale avventura grafica, gli oggetti, quei pochi che si prendono, li si prendono durante le conversazioni con alcuni personaggi, e solo in un paio di casi, specialmente nella "trasferta" c'e un barlume di avventura grafica. Il resto è solo un luuungo dialogare tra i vari personaggi fino a sbloccare ciò che ci serve per andare avanti nella piccola storia di questo gioco. La storia di questo gioco è semplice. Voi siete Duke, un pirata dal poco cervello ma molta forza, che vuole diventare capitano della nave al posto del vecchio capitano, che è caduto in mare durante i crediti iniziali. ^^; Il braccio destro del fu capitano, gli fa una proposta, per avere diritto a diventare il nuovo capitano. la proposta è questa: Trovare e far innamorare di se, 3 donne che si trovano sulla piccola isola dove si svolgerà il 95% della vostra avventura. In poche parole, hanno preso lo spunto dalla prima parte di Monkey Island 1 Ossia: Le tre prove. E ci hanno fatto un intero gioco. La difficoltà in ciò, ovviamente, è che il gigante non è bravo a parlare con le donne, non ne ha avute tante di possibilità, scappavano terrorizzate nel solo vederlo arrivare. ^^; Ma starà a voi riuscire nell'intento e farlo diventare capitano. In questo gioco ci sono molti riferimenti per non dire situazioni che richiamano i primi due capitoli di Monkey Island. Ad esempio la cella dello sceriffo è uguale al 99% della cella di Monkey Island 2, ma senza il cane. ^_^ Sia la musica che alcune situazioni richiamano i suddetti titoli. E il problema è proprio questo. Si ha l'impressione di giocare ad una semi parodia molto breve dei succitati titoli. Graficamente richiama il primo capitolo 3d della serie Monkey Island. Per il resto ? A 2 euro o poco meno, vale la pena dargli un'occhiata, ma non dovrete aspettarvi molto, come si dice: Poco paghi e poco hai. Senza dimenticare che l'unica lingua del gioco oltre l'inglese è il tedesco. Non so se mi spiego. 

Per finire, se volete un gioco per far passare un paio di ore senza problemi, enigmi inclusi, questo titolo potrebbe far per voi. Se invece volete una vera avventura grafica piuttosto duratura e con una storia e ambientazione che non rimanda ai vecchi titoli, passate oltre, qui non c' e nulla da vedere. ^_^

Terminer le jeu prends environ 3h. J'ai obtenu tous les achievements sans avoir besoin de recharger de sauvegarde. Ils sont vraiment simples, rien de caché, même s'il me semble que certains peuvent être zappés si on va directement à la solution sans tenter un peu tout ce qui est possible.

[h1]En bref[/h1]

Un point&click court mais agréable. Pour le prix, vraiment rien à redire. Recommandé !

A fairly short and straight-forward point and click. The art and animations are a little awkward, and there are only about 10 locations.  The price is more than fair for what this game has to offer.  In all, I really enjoyed it because it is fun to play and Duke is a great character.  I hope they can manage to make some more.
